# 🧭 What Is Quarto? {#what-is-quarto}

[⏱️ 0:05]{.clock}

## Quarto = Markdown → Anything {#quarto-hub}

![](assets/quarto-hub.svg){fig-alt="Two inputs, a .md Markdown file and a .qmd file with code in Python, R, bash, SQL, MATLAB, Java, JavaScript or C, flow into Quarto, shown by its four-quadrant logo, which combines Pandoc with Jupyter and knitr. Quarto produces four groups of formats: documents (html, pdf, docx, odt and, highlighted, epub); presentations (revealjs, pptx, beamer); the web (website, blog, dashboard); and more (Markdown, Jupyter notebooks, JATS, wikis)." width="92%"}

[📚 [All Quarto output formats](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/all-formats.html) ·
Quarto logo: Posit, PBC]{.source}

::: {.notes}
Pandoc converts the Markdown. Code cells run in Jupyter (Python) or knitr (R), and their
results are inserted. Quarto's principal languages are Python, R, Julia and Observable
JavaScript (`{ojs}` cells, run in the reader's browser); Jupyter kernels add many more,
such as MATLAB or Java (https://quarto.org/docs/faq/,
https://quarto.org/docs/computations/ojs.html). knitr's engines run `{sql}`, `{c}` and
`{bash}` cells (https://pkg.yihui.org/rmarkdown-book/language-engines.html); in Jupyter,
`!` lines run shell commands
(https://quarto.org/docs/computations/execution-options.html#shell-commands). Today we
use Python only. The official
list groups documents (HTML, PDF, MS Word, OpenDocument, ePub), presentations (Revealjs,
PowerPoint, Beamer), Markdown flavours, wikis and more (Jupyter, JATS, RTF, …):
https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/all-formats.html. ePub is the e-book format:
https://quarto.org/docs/reference/formats/epub.html. Websites and blogs
(https://quarto.org/docs/websites/) and dashboards (https://quarto.org/docs/dashboards/)
are built from the same files. All checked 2026-10-30. The Quarto logo is a Posit, PBC
trademark, used here to refer to Quarto (https://quarto.org/trademark.html).
:::

[🏠 before the workshop]{.pace}

::: {.cards .tips}

[🛡️]{.big}

**Once: PowerShell as admin**

Start → PowerShell → right-click → Run as administrator
:::
::: {.fragment}
[⌨️]{.big}

**`wsl --install`**

restart, open "Ubuntu", choose a username + password (typing shows nothing)
:::
::: {.fragment}
[📂]{.big}

**`pwd` · `ls` · `cd folder`**

where am I · what is here · go in (`cd ..` goes up)
:::
::: {.fragment}
[📁]{.big}

**`mkdir name`**

new folder, then `cd name`
:::
:::

Help text instead? `wsl --install -d Ubuntu` · check: `wsl -l -v` shows VERSION 2 · 🚫 blocked? Tell the organiser **before** the day

::: {.notes}
Windows only; macOS and Linux users open their own terminal. Do this at home: it needs a
download, a restart and the first Ubuntu start, which do not fit the 0:10 block. It needs
Windows 10 build 19041 or later, or Windows 11. Installing WSL needs an
administrator PowerShell once (Start menu, type PowerShell, right-click, Run as
administrator); `wsl --install` installs Ubuntu by default and needs a restart
(https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/wsl/install). If it prints help text instead (WSL
already present), run `wsl --install -d Ubuntu`; if it hangs at 0.0%, try
`wsl --install --web-download -d Ubuntu`. `wsl -l -v` must show VERSION 2. If it fails with
error 0x80370102, virtualization is off in the BIOS (Task Manager → Performance → CPU shows
"Virtualization: Enabled" when it is on), and without administrator rights it cannot be
installed at all: such participants cannot use this route, so collect them before the day
and pair them with a neighbour (no native Windows route is supported). Afterwards Ubuntu opens from the Start
menu, or type `wsl` in any PowerShell window; `exit` returns. The first Ubuntu start asks
for a Linux username and password (typing the password shows nothing: that is normal).
Every later step happens in Ubuntu, as a normal user, not as admin. The terminal opens in
your home folder `~`. `pwd` prints the current folder, `ls` lists it, `cd name` enters a
folder, `cd ..` goes up, `cd` alone returns home, `mkdir name` creates a folder. Later
slides ask you to run `mkdir -p london-guide && cd london-guide`: this is that. Tab
completes names. Written from Microsoft's documentation, checked 2026-11-03 and not yet tried on a
Windows machine: try it before teaching.
:::

## 📋 Copy and Paste in the Terminal {#terminal-copy-paste}

::: {.cards .tips}
::: {}
[🖱️]{.big}

**Mouse**

select text → right-click copies · right-click again pastes
:::
::: {.fragment}
[🐧]{.big}

**Ubuntu (WSL)**

Ctrl+Shift+C copy · Ctrl+Shift+V paste
:::
::: {.fragment}
[🟦]{.big}

**PowerShell**

Ctrl+C copy · Ctrl+V paste
:::
::: {.fragment}
[☰]{.big}

**Older console window**

title bar right-click → Edit → Copy / Paste
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .bigline}
⚠️ Ctrl+C with nothing selected stops a running command
:::

::: {.notes}
In Windows Terminal (the default on current Windows 11) the mouse works as listed: with
text selected, right-click copies it; with nothing selected, right-click pastes. Ctrl+Shift+C
and Ctrl+Shift+V work in every profile, so teach those first for Ubuntu. In PowerShell,
Ctrl+C copies only while text is selected, otherwise it interrupts, and Ctrl+V pastes. The
Edit menu is in the title-bar menu of the older console window, not Windows Terminal, where
the command palette (Ctrl+Shift+P) lists copy and paste actions. Pasting several lines runs
them: read prompts before pressing Enter. Settings differ by version and can be remapped
(https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/terminal/customize-settings/actions). Written from
Microsoft's documentation, checked 2026-11-03 and not yet tried on a Windows machine: try it before teaching. Prompts in this
deck have a copy button, which avoids selecting by hand.
:::

## 🧠 Model + 🔧 Harness = 🤖 Assistant {#model-harness}

::: {.cards .tips}
::: {}
[🧠]{.big}

**Model**

reads and writes text, asks for tools
:::
::: {}
[🔧]{.big}

**Harness**

files, commands, permissions
:::
::: {}
[🤖]{.big}

**Coding assistant**

model + harness in your terminal
:::
:::

. . .

📏 **Bigger, newer model → usually better on hard tasks**

🪶 Small models: fast, cheap, may stumble on multi-step work

✅ **Enough today:** Haiku or Sonnet on **medium** · Sol on **low**

::: {.check}
💬 Which would you pick to fix a typo, and which to join two datasets?
:::

::: {.notes}
The model is the language model (for example Claude, GPT or Gemini). The harness is the
program around it: it gives the model tools to read and write files, run commands and
search, asks you to approve actions, and feeds results back in a loop. Assistants such as the three on the next slide are harnesses; many can run several models, so the same harness behaves
differently with a different model, and the same model behaves differently in a different
harness. Size and quality matter per task: larger, more recent models usually follow
longer instructions, plan multi-step work, and recover from errors better, while small
models are quicker and cheaper and are often enough for short, well-specified edits such as
fixing a typo or reformatting a table. Hard tasks here, such as joining datasets or
debugging a failed render, reward the stronger model. Quality is not only size: training
and recency matter too, and no model is always right, so check its work (the "you
direct and check" rule). Good answer to the check: a small model for the typo, the
strongest available for the join. If a prompt keeps failing, try a stronger model inside
your assistant (see its documentation for how). Model names and availability change
often; do not name versions on stage. For this workshop the prompts are short and
well specified, so Haiku or Sonnet with the effort (reasoning) setting on medium, or
ChatGPT's Sol on low, is sufficient; try a stronger model or higher effort only if a prompt keeps failing.
:::

## 🐧 Install Tools in Ubuntu {#install-tools}

[🏠 before the workshop]{.pace} 🪟 Windows: paste in Ubuntu, one block at a time

::: {.you}
```bash
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y curl git
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
cd "$(mktemp -d)"   # downloads go here
```

```bash
R=https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/releases
V=$(curl -fsSLI -o /dev/null -w '%{url_effective}' $R/latest); V=${V##*/v}
curl -fLO $R/download/v$V/quarto-$V-linux-$(dpkg --print-architecture).deb
sudo apt install -y ./quarto-$V-linux-*.deb
```

```bash
R=https://github.com/cli/cli/releases
V=$(curl -fsSLI -o /dev/null -w '%{url_effective}' $R/latest); V=${V##*/v}
curl -fLO $R/download/v$V/gh_${V}_linux_$(dpkg --print-architecture).deb
sudo apt install -y ./gh_${V}_linux_*.deb
```
:::

🔑 `sudo` asks for your Ubuntu password (typing shows nothing) · then open a new tab

::: {.notes}
Fresh Ubuntu images may lack `curl`, so the first block installs it. `sudo` asks for the
Linux password chosen at the first start; typing shows nothing. uv's installer
(https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/) puts `uv` in `~/.local/bin`, which
only a new shell sees. Quarto has no Ubuntu apt package: the `.deb` on the GitHub release
page is the Linux route (https://quarto.org/docs/download/). Its file name contains the
version, so the block reads the latest tag from the `releases/latest` redirect (no API rate
limit on shared Wi-Fi) and `dpkg --print-architecture` picks `amd64` or `arm64` (Snapdragon
laptops). The GitHub CLI maintainers advise against Ubuntu's own `gh` package
(https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/trunk/docs/install_linux.md, which also gives an apt
repository route that updates itself); the release `.deb` used here is a one-off install.
The first block ends in a fresh temporary folder, so the `.deb` files never pile up in a
workshop folder or `/mnt/c`. Both lookups were run on 2026-11-03 (Quarto 1.11.9, gh 2.103.3) from a Mac, which proves the
URLs resolve; the `apt` lines themselves have not been tried on a Windows machine: run them
once in a fresh Ubuntu before teaching. Needs Quarto 1.10 or later. Behind a corporate proxy
these downloads can fail: tell the organiser before the day.
:::

### Exercise · ⏱️ 4 min

::: {.done}
`quarto --version` says 1.10 or newer, `uv --version` runs, `gh auth status` says "Logged in", and `~/quarto-workshop/checkpoints/` exists.

Quarto 1.10 or newer is needed (current 1.11.x); older ones fail on the London white paper
and the Typst PDF settings. `quarto check` reports Pandoc and Typst. Its Python and Jupyter lines may show "(None)", or
"Jupyter is not available" with an install hint to ignore:
each project gets its own Python environment from uv, by a prompt in each part, so there is
nothing to install for Python now. uv also downloads a Python if the computer has none.
Install uv with `curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh` (on Windows, inside
Ubuntu) or `brew install uv`: https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/
(checked 2026-10-30). Do not debug kernels on stage. A fresh Git has no identity and `git commit`
fails, hence `git config`: use the name and email of your GitHub account (or its
noreply address). Skip the `git config` lines if `git config user.name` already prints a
name. If `~/quarto-workshop` already exists, update it with `git -C ~/quarto-workshop pull`
instead of cloning, so the checkpoints and catch-up steps are current. The cloned workshop
repository supplies the checkpoints and the
water data. `gh auth status` must show a logged-in account before publishing.
PDFs use `format: typst`, bundled with Quarto, so no LaTeX is needed:
https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/typst.html. GitHub CLI install and `gh auth login`:
https://cli.github.com/ (both checked 2026-10-30).

### Exercise · ⏱️ 5 min

::: {.done}
`hello.html` and `hello.pdf` say 42, and you told the organiser.
:::

::: {.notes}
The setup check proves the tools are installed; this proves they work together, which is
what the first hour needs: the assistant is signed in, can write a file and run commands
you approve, uv builds a project environment, Quarto runs Python through it, and Typst
writes a PDF. It also fills uv's cache, so Part 1's environment step is quicker. Use
`codex` or `agy` instead of `claude` if that is your assistant. Ask participants to confirm
before the day (a reply to the invitation is enough) and follow up with anyone who has not,
or whose run failed: these are the problems that otherwise surface in the tightest block.
Every render prints `[IPKernelApp] WARNING | Kernel is running over TCP without encryption`;
in the dry run of 2026-11-01 (ipykernel 7.4) it came with every successful render and changed
nothing in the output. Tested 2026-10-31 with Quarto 1.6.40 (participants now get 1.11.x; the Quarto 1.10 or newer rule stands, so re-run it once) and uv in an empty folder
(commands run by hand, not
through an assistant). The folder is disposable: delete `~/quarto-test` afterwards. It uses
YAML, a code cell and inline code before their slides on purpose: it is a black-box check
that the tools work together, not a lesson, and the slide says Part 1 explains it.
:::

::: {.notes}
Pre-work, like the setup check: read it at home, no typing. In the room, ask who has not read it;
Part 1's first block uses exactly these constructs, one per slide, so nobody is blocked.
Page checked 2026-10-30.
:::

## 🧰 Three Boxes, Three Roles {#three-boxes}

[👀 An example: you will paste prompts like this from Part 1 on.]{.source}

::: {.prompt}
```default
Create london.md with a level-1 heading "Visit London" and one welcome paragraph.
```
:::

::: {.agent}
writes `london.md` · may run `quarto render london.md`
:::

::: {.you}
approve its commands · open `london.html` in your browser
:::

::: {.notes}
Violet: paste this prompt into your coding assistant (use the copy button).
Amber: what the assistant will probably run; you do not repeat it. Green: the few
things you type or click yourself, such as accounts, publishing and opening files. The
assistant occupies its terminal, so type green commands (such as `quarto preview`) in a
second terminal tab opened in the same folder.
The prompts are examples, not transcripts: assistants vary, so check the result.
:::

## 🧪 Prompts Are Engineered · 🔍 Ask When Unsure {#prompts-engineered}

::: {.cards .tips}
::: {}
[🧪]{.big}

**Engineered prompts**

designed with AI to reduce errors
:::
::: {}
[❓]{.big}

**Don't understand it?**

ask an AI or search the docs
:::
::: {}
[🔍]{.big}

**Dig deeper**

what it does, why, when to use it
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.prompt}
```default
Explain what a Markdown table is and when to use it. Then name the official docs page where I can verify your answer.
```
:::

::: {.notes}
The prompts in this deck were written with AI assistance and refined to reduce the chance
of errors, but they are not magic and assistants vary. Whenever a concept, option or command
is unfamiliar (a YAML key, a Markdown construct, a Python call), do not just paste and move
on: ask your assistant, or read the official documentation, to understand what it does,
why it is used and where else it applies. Understanding the details lets you spot when a
result is wrong and adapt the prompts to your own work. The prompt above is an example of
such a question; use it on any term in the deck.
:::

## 🗣️ How to Prompt Your Coding Assistant {#how-to-prompt}

::: {.cards .tips}
::: {}
[🎯]{.big}

**Be specific**

file names, columns, chart types
:::
::: {}
[☝️]{.big}

**One step at a time**

one task per prompt
:::
::: {}
[✅]{.big}

**Ask it to run & check**

"…render it and tell me about errors"
:::
::: {}
[👀]{.big}

**Check what changed**

you are responsible for the result
:::
:::

🌍 ¿Español? Your first prompt can be: `Responde siempre en español; deja el código y los nombres de archivo en inglés.`

::: {.notes}
A good prompt names the file, the content, the output and a completion check. Browser
translation translates the prompts on the slides, and the copy button copies the
translation; the file names, columns, options and commands in them stay in English, so
the assistant still finds them. You may also write your own prompts in Spanish.
Short follow-ups work once the conversation has context. Ask the assistant to show
what it changed; read the diff before moving on.
:::
